We have spent eight sections building progressively more sophisticated mixed-effects models,
but we have not yet stopped to systematically ask: how do we know a model is any good? A
model can converge, produce a tidy `summary()` table, and still be badly misspecified. This
section works through a practical diagnostic checklist, and the specific plots used to carry
each check out. Our focus here is deliberately narrow: this is about diagnostic visualization
-- plots whose job is to help you decide whether a model is trustworthy -- not about general
data visualization or building a polished figure to communicate a result to a reader. For
guidance on the latter, a dedicated data-visualization reference is a better resource than this
section.

## 9.1. What Are We Actually Checking?

Linear mixed-effects models rest on several distributional assumptions, extending the
familiar ones from ordinary regression:

1. **Additivity and Linearity**: I would more generally phrase this as the "shape" of our relationship correct. 
   That is, we can fit curvilinear regressions with polynomials but remember that 
   polynomials are additive and linear in their 
   components (e.g., `time + I(time^2)`). Bottom line, if we fit linear `time` to 
   a non-linear pattern, everything downstream from that is likely biased. 
2. **Normality of residuals**: $\epsilon_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$.
3. **Normality of random effects**: $\mathbf{b}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},
   \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b)$. The random slopes and intercepts, not just the residuals, should
   also look roughly normal.
4. **Homoscedasticity**: residual variance is roughly constant across the range of fitted
   values and predictors (Section 6 covered what to do when this fails outright).

And then we have two important *considerations* (not strictly speaking assumptions)
that we want to check:
5. **No excessive collinearity** among the fixed-effect predictors, which inflates standard
   errors and makes individual coefficients unstable even when the overall model fits well.
6. **No single subject/cluster with disproportionate influence** on the fixed-effect
   estimates.

We'll fit one example model and then work through each of these in turn.

```{r libraries, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(DHARMa)
library(influence.ME)
```

```{r fit-example-model}
set.seed(456)
n_sub <- 35
df_diag <- expand.grid(
  subID = factor(1:n_sub),
  time  = 1:4
) %>%
  mutate(
    # As in Section 7, note that group is assigned by SUBJECT (as.numeric(subID)),
    # not by row order, so that it is a genuine between-subjects grouping factor.
    group = factor(if_else(as.numeric(subID) <= n_sub / 2, "Placebo", "Drug")),
    score = 20 + 2.5 * time + 3.0 * (group == "Drug") * time +
      rnorm(n_sub, 0, 3)[subID] + rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

ggplot(data=df_diag, aes(x=time, y=score))+
  geom_point(aes(col=group), alpha=0.5)+
  stat_smooth(aes(col=group), alpha=0.5, method="lm")+
  theme_bw() +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9"))

mod_diag <- lmer(score ~ group * time + (1 + time | subID), data = df_diag)
anova(mod_diag)
```

## 2. Adding Our Residuals and Fitted Values into the Data Frame
To perform many of our diagnostic checks, it is helpful to add the fitted values and residuals
from our model back into the data. **Note the simplest tools for doing this `resid()` and `fitted()` export a vector equal in length to the number of observations that went into the model.** In practice, this means you need to be careful about any cases with missing values
that might have been dropped from the model. Usually, you will just get an error that the data frame and the vector are not the same length and cannot be added together but it is good to remember that these functions do not automatically know which observations go with which participant are time point, so you - as the user - need to make sure the rows are lining up correctly. 

As a reminder, from a mixed model, we will get residuals and two different kinds of fitted values:

* Marginal Fitted Values: Use only the models fixed effects and ignore random effects (e.g., two participants from the group with have the same marginal fitted values if Group was a fixed effect).

* Conditional Fitted Values: Use both the fixed effects and random effects to get a unique estimated value for each participants (e.g., two participants from the same group will have different conditional fitted values because conditional fitted values add their fixed and random effects together to get unique estimates for each person).

* Residuals: Residuals are the differences between our data - the actual observed values - and the fitted values. Typically, we are interested in the **conditional residuals** (i.e., the difference between the data and each unique estimate) but we can also calculate **marginal residuals** (i.e., the difference between the data and the fixed effects only). 


```{r fitted-values}
# ---- Add fitted values and residuals to the data ----------------------------
# lmer gives two kinds of fitted values and residuals:
#   * Conditional: use the fixed effects AND the subject's own random effects
#       fitted = X*b + Z*u ;  residual = y - X*b - Z*u   (level-1 residuals)
#   * Marginal: use the fixed effects only
#       fitted = X*b       ;  residual = y - X*b         (subject deviations + noise)
# The level-1 assumptions (constant variance, normality) are about the
# CONDITIONAL residuals. Marginal residuals are useful for checking whether
# the population-average trajectory is right.
df_diag <- df_diag %>%
  mutate(
    fit_cond   = fitted(mod_diag),                # X*b + Z*u
    res_cond   = resid(mod_diag),                 # y - (X*b + Z*u)
    fit_marg   = predict(mod_diag, re.form = NA), # X*b only
    res_marg   = score - fit_marg,
    # Standardized conditional residuals: residual / sigma
    res_std    = res_cond / sigma(mod_diag)
  )
```


## 2. Do we have the "shape" of the data correct? 
Using these fitted values and residuals, we can do several checks to make sure we have the "shape" of the data correct. 

**First, we can create a residuals versus fitted values plot** in which we plot the conditional residuals on the y-axis against the conditional fitted values on the x-axis. If we have the shape of the relationship (alternatively "functional form") correct, then there should be no real pattern to the residuals. If we see a clear pattern in the residuals (e.g., U-shape or n-shape) that would suggest there is some non-linearity in the data we are not accounting for (e.g., we fit linear function for `time` and instead should fit a quadratic, `time+I(time^2)`.

``` {r resid v fitted plot}
# 1. Residuals vs. fitted values ----------------------------------------------
# We want a flat, patternless band centered on zero. A curve (U shape or
# arch) suggests a wrong functional form, such as a missing quadratic term.
p_res_fit <- ggplot(df_diag, aes(x = fit_cond, y = res_cond)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "1. Residuals vs. fitted",
       x = "Fitted values (conditional)", y = "Residual (conditional)")
p_res_fit
```

The residuals versus fitted plot combines the contributions of all fixed and random effects into a single fitted value. That makes it a convenient overall check, especially for whether residual variance changes with the predicted mean. But collapsing everything onto one axis can also hide problems: a misspecified effect of one predictor can be diluted or cancelled by the others. Plotting residuals against each predictor separately is a more sensitive check of functional form, and plotting them against one predictor within levels of another (here, `time` within `group`) checks additivity.

Note that our assumptions about shape really only applies to the continuous predictor and it's interactions (e.g., for a categorical factor, we will estimate a unique mean for every level, so we cannot really get the shape of it's mean structure wrong). When we shift to just `time` as a specific predictor, we will also switch to the marginal residuals. Using conditional residuals here wouldn’t be wrong, but it could mislead: the subject-level random effects can absorb some misspecification and make it look as though we’ve captured the shape of `time` better than we have. Broadly, marginal residuals are the natural choice for checking the fixed part of the model, and conditional residuals for checking the error assumptions at the lowest level of the data. 

In the plot below, we are interested in a few things. First, is the mean of the residuals generally close to zero across time? This suggests we got the shape of time correct. Second, do we see a similar pattern in the mean of the residuals in both groups? This suggests the same shape of time applies to both groups. And third, do we see any difference in the **variance** of the residuals across time? This is our first check into the **heteroskedasticity** of the residuals. 

``` {r residuals v predictors plot}
# 2. Residuals vs. predictors -------------------------------------------------
# Same idea, but against each predictor, here time separately by group.
# Using the MARGINAL residuals asks: "Does the population-average line for each
# group follow the data at every time point?" Mean marginal residuals that
# drift away from 0 at certain times mean the trajectory shape is wrong.
p_res_time <- ggplot(df_diag, aes(x = time, y = res_marg)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", colour = "firebrick", size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  labs(title = "2. Marginal residuals vs. time, by group",
       x = "Time", y = "Residual (marginal)")
p_res_time
```
Finally, it helps to plot the observed trajectories (a spaghetti plot of each participant’s data over `time`) against the trajectories implied by the model (the group-average lines from our fixed effects). This plot asks two questions. First, does the model’s average trajectory match the overall shape of the data? Second, do the individual trajectories vary in ways the model can represent?

Suppose most participants follow a roughly linear path and the model estimates a linear trend: good agreement. But suppose many participants level off or tail downward at later time points. Then the average trajectory isn’t linear, and the fixed effect of time is misspecified; we may need a quadratic or spline term. The same is true if the curvature shows up in one group but not the other: the model is missing a group-by-curvature interaction. 

If we have tested a series of unconditional models on the front-end, this can often be a more confirmatory step (e.g., linear slopes led to the lowest AIC and we see agreement in linear slopes). However, because we often choose the shape of `time` in unconditional models on the front-end, we can now check that it still accurately reflects each group on the back-end once all moderators are accounted for.


```{r observed versus implied trjectories}
# 3. Observed vs. model-implied trajectories ----------------------------------
# Thin lines show each subject's observed data. Thick lines show the
# fixed-effect (population-average) prediction for each group. Model and data
# should follow the same overall shape.
p_traj <- ggplot(df_diag, aes(x = time, y = score)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = subID), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit_marg, colour = group), linewidth = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ group) +
  labs(title = "3. Observed trajectories and fixed-effect predictions",
       x = "Time", y = "Score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_traj
```



## 3. Assumptions about the Random Parts of the Model 
We can check **homoskedasticity** (i.e., similar variance) by creating a scale-location plot. 
In this figure, we plot the absolute value of the standardized residuals against the conditional fitted values. As before, we are hoping to see no clear pattern to these residuals. 

Additionally, we can plot our conditional residuals at the specific levels of our fixed effects, by `group` in this case. If one group showed massively larger residual variance than the other group, that would suggest we need a more complicated model (i.e., at present our model assumes that a single residual variance applies equally to both groups).

```{r scale location plot}
# 4. Homoscedasticity (scale-location plot) -----------------------------------
# Plot sqrt(|standardized residual|) against fitted values. If the variance is
# constant, the smoothed line is roughly flat. A funnel or upward trend means
# the residual variance increases with the mean.
# Also check the variance by group, because the model assumes ONE sigma
# shared by both groups.
p_scale_loc <- ggplot(df_diag, aes(x = fit_cond, y = sqrt(abs(res_std)))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "4a. Scale-location",
       x = "Fitted values (conditional)",
       y = expression(sqrt("|standardized residual|")))
p_scale_loc

p_var_group <- ggplot(df_diag, aes(x = group, y = res_cond)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "4b. Residual spread by group", x = NULL, y = "Residual (conditional)")
p_var_group
```

Next, we can check the normality of our residuals using a quantile-quantile ("QQ") normal plot. In this plot we show the quantiles observed in the sample against the hypothetical quantiles we would observe if the data were perfectly normal. 
```{r normality of residuals}
# 5. Normality of level-1 residuals -------------------------------------------
# QQ plot of standardized conditional residuals. Points should lie close to
# the line. Heavy tails show up as an S shape, and skew as a curve.
# (In larger samples, mild non-normality here matters much less than errors
# in the mean structure.)
p_qq_resid <- ggplot(df_diag, aes(sample = res_std)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "5. QQ plot: level-1 residuals",
       x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles")
p_qq_resid
```

We can make equivalent plots of all of our random effects. The only notable difference will be that we should have fewer observations in these QQ plots. For instance, if I had 10 observations for 10 participants, my residual plot with have 100 data points, but a QQ plot of the random intercepts/slopes would only have 10 data points.
```{r normality of random effects}
# 6. Normality of the random effects ------------------------------------------
# One point per SUBJECT, so there are only n_sub points per panel. Expect
# some wobble. We are looking for gross departures or a single extreme
# subject.
# Caveat: BLUPs are shrunken toward 0 and can look "more normal" than the
# true random-effect distribution, so this check has limited power.
re_df <- ranef(mod_diag)$subID %>%
  as_tibble(rownames = "subID") %>%
  pivot_longer(-subID, names_to = "term", values_to = "blup")

p_qq_re <- ggplot(re_df, aes(sample = blup)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "6. QQ plots: random effects (BLUPs)",
       x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "BLUP")
p_qq_re
```

Two things to keep in mind when checking the normality assumption:

1. This only applies to our "traditional" linear mixed effects model in which normality of the residuals and random-effects is assumed. For other models (e.g., ordinal models, logistic models), the normality assumption might only apply to the random effects or to neither. So, although we will probably be checking against normality most of the time, remember the key thing is to check the assumptions specific to your model. It is just that most of the time we are assuming normality. 

2. Many learners want to reach for hypothesis tests as a way of getting a clear "go / no-go" decision about normality (e.g., Kruskil-Wallis or Shaprio-Wilk tests), but I would generally discourage this way of thinking about parametric assumptions. First, these tests are subject to many different vulnerabilities (e.g., low power an you miss non-normality or extreme sensitivity and you reject trivial non-normality in large samples). Second, violating normality happens on a continuum and so do its effects (i.e., our predictions get more wrong the less our assumptions hold, there is not a clear threshold at which we are right or wrong). Third, assuming that our other assumptions hold, linear mixed effect models are generally robust to violations of normality. So, unless you have extremely non-normal residuals - in which case you should probably reach for a different type of model - minor deviations from normality probably won't appreciably affect your fixed effect estimates or statistical inferences. 


## 4. Checking Your Data
**Collinearity** arises when predictors in our model are correlated. Some degree of collinearity is to be expected, but high degrees of collinearity are problematic. For instance, imagine that I have `height` and `weight` in the model. Taller people tend to be heavier, on average, but the correlation is modest, so it will make sense to "control for" one variable when talking about the other (e.g., are you heavy for your height?). In contrast, imagine that by accident I put `height` in inches and `height_cm` in centimeters into my model. These two variables are perfectly correlated, so cannot "control for" one without completely removing the other (i.e., all of the variance in inches is already explained by centimeters and vice versa).

A common way to check collinearity is by calculating **variance inflation factors (VIF)**. As the name suggest, VIF shows how much the variance for one term is inflated based on the presence of other terms in the model. Ideally, we would like variance inflation factors close to 1.o (i.e., no inflation). In practice, VIF is most problematic when it gets above 4 or 5. 

```{r collinearity}
# 7. Collinearity: VIF computed from the fixed-effect covariance matrix -------
# In OLS, VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R^2_j). For a mixed model we can get an equivalent
# value from the correlations among the fixed-effect estimates: drop the
# intercept, convert vcov() to a correlation matrix, invert it, and take the
# diagonal. (This is what car::vif() does for merMod objects.)
vif_by_hand <- function(model) {
  V <- as.matrix(vcov(model))
  V <- V[-1, -1, drop = FALSE]          # drop the intercept
  R <- cov2cor(V)                       # correlations among the estimates
  setNames(diag(solve(R)), colnames(R)) # VIF_j = [R^-1]_jj
}
vif_by_hand(mod_diag)
```

Looking our VIFs above, the largest is <3, which is below our cut-off of 4 or 5, but this is good teachable moment to reinforce a lesson from **Section 05**: the VIF we are seeing here is an artifact of how we coded the data, it is not an essential or irreducible collinearity. To see this is brief, we will mean-center our time variable and code group using orthogonal polynomials. For a more detailed explanation see **Section 05**. 

```{r essential collinearity}
# Teaching point: part of the correlation between the 'group' main effect and
# the group x time interaction is "nonessential" collinearity. It comes from
# coding, not from the data: 'time' runs 1-4, so 0 lies outside the observed
# range. Centering time moves the group main effect to the middle of the study
# and lowers those VIFs. The VIFs here are modest to begin with (all < 2.5);
# the effect is much bigger when time is far from 0, e.g. coded as age in
# years. The model fit is identical; only the meaning of the lower-order
# terms changes.

df_diag <- df_diag %>% mutate(time_c = time - mean(time))
contrasts(df_diag$group) <- contr.poly(nlevels(df_diag$group))
mod_diag_c <- lmer(score ~ group * time_c + (1 + time_c | subID), data = df_diag)
vif_by_hand(mod_diag_c)
c(logLik_raw = logLik(mod_diag), logLik_centered = logLik(mod_diag_c)) # same fit
```
Simply by changing how we coded our data, this dropped all of the collinearities to 1.0, illustrating that this collinearity was an artifact and not essential to our model. 

In contrast, consider psychologist trying to measure anxiety and depression in a sample of people. These constructs have considerable overlap (e.g., anxious people are more depressed and depressed people are more anxious) and will therefore be collinear in our statistical model. However, this collinearity is essential to what those data actually are (i.e., it reflects a fundamental property of anxiety and depression) not an artifact of how we have coded the data. 


Next, we can check for *influential data points* that might have undue sway on our model. It is easiest to think about this influential data points as outliers (on either X or Y) that pull the models predictions in their direction. The most famous example of this - an beautiful way to see many of these regression diagnostics - is a dataset called [Anscombe's Quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anscombe%27s_quartet). For our purposes, I will show how to calculate a statistic called [Cook's Distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%27s_distance) as a way of identifying overly influential individuals in our mixed model. 

```{r cooks distance}
# 8. Influential subjects and data points -------------
## Subject level: refits the model 35 times, once per subID left out
mod_lme4 <- lme4::lmer(score ~ group * time + (1 + time | subID), data = df_diag)


infl_subj <- stats::influence(mod_lme4, groups = "subID")
cd_subj   <- cooks.distance(infl_subj)
dfb_subj  <- dfbetas(infl_subj)

infl_obs  <- stats::influence(mod_lme4, ncores = 4)
cd_obs    <- cooks.distance(infl_obs)

subj_ids <- as.character(unique(df_diag$subID))  # order influence() deleted subjects

## 1. Cook's D by subject
tibble(subID = subj_ids, cooksd = cd_subj) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(subID, -cooksd), y = cooksd)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Subject", y = "Cook's D") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, size = 7))

## 2. Cook's D by observation
tibble(row = seq_along(cd_obs), cooksd = cd_obs) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = row, y = cooksd)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Observation (row)", y = "Cook's D") +
  theme_bw()

## 3. DFBETAS by subject, one panel per fixed effect
as.data.frame(dfb_subj) |>
  mutate(subID = subj_ids) |>
  pivot_longer(-subID, names_to = "term", values_to = "dfbetas") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = subID, y = dfbetas)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ term) +
  labs(x = "Subject", y = "DFBETAS") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, size = 7))
```
